In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He asked about the absence of expansion in a way that denies it, so the question establishes and affirms the expansion. It is as if it were said: "We expanded your breast for you." For this reason, the verb "We placed down" is joined to it, taking the meaning into account. As for the meaning of "We expanded your breast": we widened it until it encompassed the universality of prophethood and the call to both the two weighty groups (humans and jinn). Or, until it bore the hardships that your people's unbelievers and others inflicted upon you. Or, we widened it with the knowledge and wisdom We deposited in it, and We removed from it the constriction and distress that accompany blindness and ignorance.

It is reported from al-Hasan: "It was filled with wisdom and knowledge." It is reported from Abu Ja'far al-Mansur that he recited ﴿Alam nashrah laka﴾ with a fatha on the ha'. They said: perhaps he pronounced the ha' between the two vowels and prolonged it in its articulation, so the listener thought he had given it a fatha.

"The burden that broke his back": "broke" here means made it collapse, the sound of breaking apart and separation under its weight. It is a parable for what weighed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and distressed him of his lapses before prophethood, or of his ignorance of the rulings and laws, or of his eagerness for the conversion of the most stubborn of his people and his anguish over them. "Placing it down from him" means: He forgave him, or taught him the laws, or cleared his excuse after he had delivered and conveyed the message.

Anas recited: "wa-hallalna wa-hatatna" (we eased and we lightened). Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-hallalna 'anka wizraka" (we eased from you your burden).

"And We raised your mention": this means He joined your name with the Name of God in the testimony of faith, the call to prayer, the iqamah (the second call to prayer), the tashahhud, and the sermons; and in other passages of the Qur'an, such as ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ and ﴿Whoever obeys God and His Messenger﴾ and ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger﴾; and in calling him "Messenger of God" and "Prophet of God"; and among this is his mention in the books of the earlier peoples, and the covenant taken from the prophets and their communities that they should believe in him.

If you ask: what is the benefit of the addition of "laka" (for you), when the meaning is complete without it? I answer: in the addition of "laka" there is what is in the method of ambiguity and clarification. It is as if it were said: "Did We not expand?" so it is understood that there is something expanded; then it is said "your breast," so what was known in ambiguous form is made clear. And likewise with ﴿laka dhikraka﴾ and ﴿'anka wizraka﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 94, verses 5–6:

If you ask: how is His saying ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ connected to what precedes it? I answer: The polytheists used to taunt the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers with poverty and hardship, until it occurred to him that they had turned away from Islam because its adherents were poor and held in contempt. So He reminded him of the great blessings He had bestowed upon him, and then said: ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾, as if He said: "We have granted you what We have granted you, so do not despair of God's bounty, for with the hardship you are in there is ease."

If you ask: "maʿa" (with) in ﴿inna maʿa﴾ denotes companionship, so what is meant by the ease and the hardship being companions? I answer: He intended that God would give them ease after the hardship they were in, within a short time. So He brought the anticipated ease close, making it as though it accompanied the hardship, as an increase in consolation and in strengthening hearts.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with them: "No hardship will overcome two eases"? [[The hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas: I have not found it. I say: al-Farraʾ mentioned it from al-Kalbi from Ibn Salih from him.]] It has also been transmitted with a raised chain (marfuʿ) that he (ﷺ) went out one day laughing and saying: "No hardship will overcome two eases." [[It was narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Maʿmar from Ayyub from al-Hasan as a mursal (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion). By his chain it was narrated by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman. al-Tabari narrated it through Abu Thawr from Maʿmar. It has another chain, narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through the narration of ʿAtiyya from Jabir as a mawsul (continuous) report, but its isnad is weak. On this subject there is also a report from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, which Malik mentioned in al-Muwatta from Zayd ibn Aslam from his father: that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab was informed that Abu ʿUbayda was in al-Sham, and he related the story, and in the letter to him he said: "No hardship will overcome two eases." It was also narrated by al-Hakim through this chain, and this is its most authentic chain.]] I say: This is to be taken according to its apparent meaning, based on the strength of hope, and that God's promise is not to be understood except as what its wording can bear and in its most eloquent sense. It is also said that the second clause may be a repetition of the first, as He repeated His saying ﴿So woe on that day to the deniers﴾ to fix its meaning in souls and establish it in hearts, just as a noun is repeated in your saying "Zayd came to me, Zayd." And it may be that the first is a promise that hardship is inevitably followed by ease, and the second is a new promise that hardship is followed by ease. In that case there are two eases, on the assumption that the second is a new statement. The hardship is one because it is either definite by reference to a known thing, namely the hardship they were in, so it is the same one, since its ruling is like that of Zayd in your saying "Indeed with Zayd is wealth, indeed with Zayd is wealth." Or it is definite for the genus that everyone knows, and it is also the same one. As for ease, it is indefinite and covers part of the genus. So if the second statement is a new statement and not a repetition, it covers a part other than the first part, without any difficulty.

If you ask: what is meant by "two eases"? I answer: It is permissible that they mean the conquests that were made easy for them in the days of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what was made easy for them in the days of the caliphs [[His saying "and what was made easy for them in the days of the caliphs" is perhaps: "and what is made easy", in the present tense. (ʿ)]], or that they mean the ease of this world and the ease of the Hereafter, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾, and they are the best outcome of victory and the best outcome of reward.

If you ask: what is the purpose of this indefiniteness? I answer: magnification. It is as if it were said: "Indeed with hardship there is ease, a great ease, and what an ease!" It occurs once in the codex of Ibn Masʿud. If you ask: since it is established in his recitation without repetition, why did he say: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, even if hardship were in a lizard's burrow, ease would pursue it until it enters upon it: no hardship will overcome two eases"? [[The hadith of Ibn Masʿud: It was narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Jaʿfar ibn Sulayman from Maymun Abu Hamza from Ibrahim from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "If hardship were in the burrow of a lizard, ease would follow it until it extracts it: no hardship will overcome two eases."]] I answer: He intended by "two eases" what is in His saying "ease" (yusran) of the meaning of magnification, so he interpreted it as the ease of the two abodes, and these are in reality two eases.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 94, verse 7–8:

If you say: How is His saying ﴿So when you are free, then labour hard﴾ connected to what precedes it? I say: When He enumerated to him His past blessings and His promise just mentioned, He prompted him to give thanks, to strive in worship and to exert himself in it, and to link one part of it to another, to follow on and to be keen not to leave any of his times empty of it. So when he is free from one act of worship, he occupies himself with another. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "So when you are free from your prayer, strive in supplication." It is related from al-Hasan: "So when you are free from the raid, strive in worship." It is related from Mujahid: "So when you are free from your worldly affairs, labour in your prayer." It is related from al-Shaʿbi that he saw a man lifting a stone, and said: "This is not what the free person is commanded to do." The sitting of a man idle, free of occupation, or his occupying himself with what does not concern him in his religion or his worldly life, is from foolishness of judgment, feebleness of intellect, and the dominance of heedlessness. Indeed ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I dislike to see any of you idle and unoccupied, neither in the work of this world nor in the work of the Hereafter." [[I did not find it. Ahmad, Ibn al-Mubarak and al-Bayhaqi all related it in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Shaybah from the route of al-Musayyib ibn Rafiʿ, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: "I truly detest a man whom I see idle, having no part in any work of this world or the Hereafter."]] Abu al-Sammal recited "farragta" with a kasra on the ra', but it is not eloquent. Among the innovations is what is related from some of the Rafidah, that he recited "fa-nsib" with a kasra on the ṣad, meaning "fa-nsib ʿAliyyan" (set up ʿAli) for the imamate. Even if this were authentic from the Rafidi, it would be valid for the Nasibi to recite it thus, taking it as a command to "nasb", which is the hatred and enmity of ʿAli. [[His saying "bi-l-naṣb" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: nasabtu li-fulān naṣban: if I opposed him.]] ﴿And to your Lord turn with desire﴾: make your desire directed to Him specifically, and ask only for His bounty, relying upon Him. It has been read: "fa-rgab", meaning: make people desire to seek what is with Him.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Alam Nashrah, it is as if he came to me while I was distressed, and he relieved me."
[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Sulaym al-Zuhri related it in al-Birr from him as a mursal report.]]
